props.title: Tex

sections.content: Tex (1982) stands as one of Disney's most grounded and authentic teenage dramas, marking a bold departure from their typical family fare. Based on S.E. Hinton's novel, this coming-of-age story shares DNA with other vital 80s teen films like The Outsiders (1983) and Rumble Fish (1983), both also Hinton adaptations directed by Francis Ford Coppola. Matt Dillon delivers a remarkably nuanced performance as Tex McCormick, capturing the raw emotional landscape of a 15-year-old struggling with abandonment, poverty, and identity in rural Oklahoma.

sections.content: Director Tim Hunter crafts a distinctly American portrait of teenage life that influenced later works like What's Eating Gilbert Grape (1993) and October Sky (1999). The film's honest portrayal of economic hardship and family dysfunction set it apart from the glossier teen films of the 1980s like Sixteen Candles (1984) or The Breakfast Club (1985). The relationship between Tex and his older brother Mason (Jim Metzler) explores themes of responsibility and sacrifice with remarkable subtlety. SUBHEAD: The Disney Renaissance of Teen Drama

Tex helped pave the way for Disney's brief but significant foray into serious teenage storytelling in the early 1980s. This movement included films like Old Yeller (1957) and later influenced works such as Stand By Me (1986). The film's success demonstrated that young audiences could handle complex themes when presented with authenticity and respect. Hunter's direction avoids melodrama, instead focusing on quiet moments and natural dialogue that feel remarkably contemporary even today.
